sec:surreal-construction-grading-intro: Conway's construction grades the surreals by birthday. This section connects the grading to the brane-tower level filtration.
def:birthday-grading:
Definition Birthday grading on a surreal-coefficient category. Let K be a real-closed field extending \mathbb{R} (typically K = \mathbf{No}, Conway's surreal numbers). The birthday b(x) \in \mathrm{Ord} of x \in \mathbf{No} is the least ordinal stage at which x is constructed in Conway's recursive \{L \mid R\} presentation.

Let \mathbf{C} be a K-linear category. The birthday grading on \mathbf{C} is the ordinal-indexed filtration of each hom-space

  \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y)_{\leq \alpha} = \bigl\{ f \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y) : \text{every coefficient of } f \text{ has birthday} \leq \alpha \bigr\}.
rem:birthday-grading-remark:
Remark Birthdays as sign-sequence lengths, and properties of the grading. Equivalently, the birthday b(x) is the length of the sign-sequence representation for x:

  b(0) = 0, \qquad b(n) = n \text{ for } n \in \mathbb{N}, \qquad b(\omega) = \omega, \qquad b(1/2) = 2, \qquad b(\pi) = \omega, \qquad b(\varepsilon) = \omega.

The birthday function refines the archimedean norm. Distinct reals x, y \in \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbf{No} have b(x), b(y) \leq \omega. The elements \varepsilon, \omega, and \omega^2 have progressively larger birthdays.

The birthday grading satisfies three properties:

  1. Exhaustiveness: \bigcup_\alpha \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y)_{\leq \alpha} = \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y).
  2. Composition: If f \in \mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)_{\leq \alpha} and g \in \mathrm{Hom}(Y,Z)_{\leq \beta}, then g \circ f \in \mathrm{Hom}(X,Z)_{\leq \alpha \oplus \beta} (where \oplus is the natural sum of ordinals).
  3. Monoidality: If \mathbf{C} is monoidal, f \otimes g \in \mathrm{Hom}(X \otimes X', Y \otimes Y')_{\leq \alpha \oplus \beta}.
rem:birthday-grading-archimedean:
Remark Birthday grading as a depth gauge and its archimedean sub-category. The birthday grading provides a coarse depth gauge for morphisms in surreal-enriched categories. It stratifies formal parameters into nested levels of infinitesimal and transfinite resolution. Statements with hom-coefficients of birthday < \omega involve only dyadic rationals. Birthday-\leq \omega statements include limit reals and first-order infinitesimals. Birthday > \omega statements use named infinities like \omega or transseries terms like \log \omega.

The sub-category defined by b(f) \leq \omega forms the archimedean-coefficient sub-category. Its morphisms have coefficients that are real numbers or bounded infinitesimals. For \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}_{\mathbf{No}}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)) with q \in \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbf{No}, this recovers \mathrm{Rep}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)). The arithmetic of \mathbf{No} restricted to birthday \leq \omega coincides with \mathbb{R} exactly on the archimedean part.
ex:birthday-grading-aether:
Example Birthday of the aether parameters c_q, \hbar_q, d_H(q) at q = 1 + \varepsilon. Consider the aether parameter q = 1 + \varepsilon for an infinitesimal \varepsilon \in \mathbf{No} with b(\varepsilon) = \omega. Its sign sequence (+, -, -, -, \ldots) has length 1 + \omega = \omega. The associated parameters resolve as follows:

  • c_q = 1/(q - 1) = 1/\varepsilon = \omega has birthday \omega.
  • \hbar_q = (q-1)/q = \varepsilon(1 + \varepsilon)^{-1} has birthday \omega.
  • d_H(q) = (2q-1)^2/q^3 = (1 + 2\varepsilon)^2(1 + \varepsilon)^{-3} has birthday \omega.

Expressions rational in q evaluated at q = 1 + \varepsilon remain in the birthday-\leq \omega stratum, embedding into the Laurent-series field \mathbb{R}(\!(\varepsilon)\!). The standard-part map distinguishes between finite and infinitesimal within this stratum. The birthday alone does not, as limit reals like \pi also have birthday \omega.
def:sign-sequence-of-braid:
Definition Sign-sequence functor B_n \to \mathbf{No} via Hecke eigenspaces. Let V be the fundamental representation of \mathrm{SU}_q(2), and let \beta = \sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1} \cdots \sigma_{i_k}^{\epsilon_k} be a braid word in B_n. Fix a standard tableau t of shape \lambda \vdash n with \ell(\lambda) \leq 2. The sign-sequence surreal \mathrm{surr}(\beta, t) \in \mathbf{No} of \beta at t is constructed as follows.

The Hecke representation \rho_n : B_n \to H_n(q) sends each \sigma_i^{\pm 1} to \sigma_i^{\pm 1}. The Hoefsmit seminormal vector v_t \in S_\lambda at t is an eigenvector of every Young--Jucys--Murphy element. The braid \beta acts on v_t by successively decomposing \rho(\sigma_{i_j}^{\epsilon_j})\, v_{t_j} into symmetric and antisymmetric components, recording s_j = + for the symmetric component and s_j = - for the antisymmetric. The resulting sign sequence s = (s_1, \ldots, s_k) defines the finite-birthday surreal \mathrm{surr}(\beta, t) := \mathrm{Gonshor}(s) \in \mathbf{No}, where \mathrm{Gonshor}: \{+, -\}^* \to \mathbf{No} is the canonical sign-sequence-to-surreal map.
rem:sign-sequence-of-braid-remark: Remark Multiplicativity and tableau independence of the sign-sequence surreal. For each fixed standard tableau t, the sign-sequence surreal assignment \mathrm{surr}(-, t) : B_n \to \mathbf{No} is a multiplicative monoid map: \mathrm{surr}(\beta_1 \beta_2, t) is computed by first applying \beta_2's sign sequence at t to obtain t', then concatenating with \beta_1's sign sequence at t'. Changing the tableau permutes the sign sequence by a Young--Jucys--Murphy permutation. Quotienting by this action gives a tableau-independent functor \widetilde{\mathrm{surr}} : B_n \longrightarrow \mathbf{No} / \sim.
rem:sign-sequence-of-braid-invariant:
Remark The sign-sequence functor as a transfinite refinement of the crossing number. A surreal number x \in \mathbf{No} admits a canonical sign-sequence presentation: a function s_x : \alpha \to \{+, -\} for some ordinal \alpha = b(x). The sequence encodes Conway's \{L \mid R\} construction step-by-step: at stage \beta < \alpha, s_x(\beta) = + means "x is the rightmost option", and s_x(\beta) = - means "leftmost option". Hecke generators have two eigenvalues, q (symmetric channel) and -q^{-1} (antisymmetric channel) (Hoefsmit seminormal form). This binary choice at each level is exactly the sign-sequence data, providing a canonical functor from braid words to surreals.

The sign sequence has length equal to the crossing number c(\beta), so b(\mathrm{surr}(\beta, t)) \leq c(\beta). Equality holds when the braid is reduced. This cleanly refines the crossing-number invariant by an ordinal-valued quantity.

The sign sequence carries strictly more information than the crossing number: it records which eigenchannel is chosen at each crossing. Distinct braids with the same crossing number generally give distinct surreals. Surrealisation is a stronger braid invariant valued in \mathbf{No} / \sim. It is the precise sense in which "Hoefsmit seminormal form is the surreal \{L \mid R\} construction".
prop:hoefsmit-is-surreal-construction:
Proposition Hoefsmit seminormal form is Conway's \{L \mid R\} construction. The Hoefsmit seminormal form (Hoefsmit seminormal form) diagonalises H_n(q) on V^{\otimes n} along a Young--Jucys--Murphy tower indexed by standard tableaux, each generator \sigma_i splitting a tableau-vector into a symmetric (q-eigen) and an antisymmetric (-q^{-1}-eigen) component. Writing \mathrm{Tab}(\lambda) for the standard tableaux of shape \lambda and \mathbf{No}_{\leq n}^{\mathrm{dy}} for the dyadic surreals of birthday \leq n, there is a canonical injective embedding

  \Phi : \bigsqcup_{\lambda \vdash n,\, \ell(\lambda) \leq 2} \mathrm{Tab}(\lambda) \hookrightarrow \mathbf{No}_{\leq n}^{\mathrm{dy}}

such that:

  1. The empty tableau at n = 0 and the singleton tableau at n = 1 both map to 0. For n \geq 2, the one-row tableau (n) maps to a non-zero value determined by its sign sequence.
  2. Each YJM-edge t \to t' in the tableau forest corresponds to a unique sign-sequence extension s \to s\!\cdot\! + (symmetric channel) or s \to s\!\cdot\! - (antisymmetric channel). The sign sequence of a size-n tableau has length n - 1.
  3. The birthday b(\Phi(t)) is bounded by the length of the sign sequence (i.e., by n - 1). Surreals in the image are of birthday \leq n - 1. The complement of the image in \mathbf{No}_{\leq n}^{\mathrm{dy}} consists of non-tableau dyadic rationals.

The eigencomponent recursion, the tableau-forest counting, and the consequences of this identification (birthday-refined crossing number, the Conway-recipe form of \rho_\lambda(\sigma_i), and the surreal sign-sequence expansion of J_K(q)) are recorded in the context note.
conj:jones-birthday:
Conjecture Birthday refinement of the Jones polynomial. The Jones polynomial J_K(q) \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1/2}] is the Markov trace \mathrm{tr}_M(\rho_n(\beta)) of the Hecke representation of any braid word \beta whose closure is the oriented link K. The Markov trace is computed by summing contributions from every standard tableau t of every two-rowed shape \lambda \vdash n.

By Hoefsmit-is-surreal-construction, each tableau t corresponds to a finite-dyadic surreal \Phi(t) \in \mathbf{No} of birthday \leq n. This suggests that the Jones polynomial admits a birthday refinement: a finer invariant that records contributions stratified by the birthday of the underlying surreal sign sequence.

There exists a refinement \widetilde{J}_K \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1/2}]^{\mathrm{Ord}} satisfying:

  1. Recovery of Jones: \sum_\alpha \widetilde{J}_K(\alpha) = J_K(q).
  2. Birthday locality: \widetilde{J}_K(\alpha) depends only on tableau contributions of YJM depth \leq \alpha.
  3. Strict refinement: there exist knots K_1, K_2 with J_{K_1}(q) = J_{K_2}(q) but \widetilde{J}_{K_1} \neq \widetilde{J}_{K_2}.

If (3) holds, \widetilde{J}_K is a strictly stronger invariant than the Jones polynomial, contradicting the classical view that all braid-word information is collapsed by the Markov trace.

The Jones polynomial loses information due to Markov-trace averaging and tableau-shape averaging. The birthday refinement preserves the trace-type averaging but stratifies by YJM depth, a finer invariant than the shape. Contributions from early symmetric channels are separated from contributions from late symmetric channels. Precedents exist: Khovanov homology categorifies the Jones polynomial and is strictly stronger. The birthday refinement exposes previously hidden tableau-level data.

To prove the conjecture, it suffices to produce two knots with identical Jones polynomials and distinct birthday refinements. To disprove it, it suffices to show that the YJM-depth filtration of any tableau contributes only via its endpoint (the shape \lambda). The proposed test is the Conway--Kinoshita pair (11n34, 11n42).

The conjecture remains open. The Hoefsmit eigenchannel data is explicit, so the refinement is computable. A direct computational attack involves computing \widetilde{J}_K for 11n34 and 11n42. For each YJM-extension path \pi of length 11, compute the Hoefsmit matrix product, convert to a sign sequence, and compute the Gonshor surreal. Aggregate contributions by b(\mathrm{Gonshor}(\pi)) to yield \widetilde{J}_K. If \widetilde{J}_{11n34} \neq \widetilde{J}_{11n42}, the conjecture is established. This requires Hoefsmit matrix entries for H_{11}(q), the gonshor map, and a script computing matrix products along YJM paths. Falsification requires proving the Hoefsmit-trajectory sum factors through the YJM endpoint.
rem:hoefsmit-is-surreal-construction-con:
Remark Hoefsmit-as-surreal — eigencomponent recursion, tableau counting, and consequences. At each step of the Young--Jucys--Murphy tower, a Hecke generator \sigma_i splits a tableau-vector into two eigencomponents:

  • the symmetric (q-eigen) component, corresponding to the tableau where boxes i and i+1 lie in the same row;
  • the antisymmetric (-q^{-1}-eigen) component, corresponding to the tableau where they lie in the same column.

This is structurally identical to Conway's recursive surreal construction.

Let \mathrm{Tab}(\lambda) denote the set of standard tableaux of shape \lambda, viewed as the vertex set of a tree \mathcal{T}_n whose edges record the Young--Jucys--Murphy ordering. Let \mathbf{No}_{= n}^{\mathrm{dy}} denote the set of dyadic surreals of birthday exactly n (equivalently, sign sequences of length n). The number of two-rowed standard tableaux of size n is \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}; the number of dyadic surreals of birthday exactly n is 2^n. The embedding \Phi of Hoefsmit seminormal form is Conway's \{L \mid R\} construction is an injective embedding, not a bijection of forests.

This identification has several immediate consequences. The sign-sequence braid invariant is well-defined and lives in \mathbf{No}_{\leq c(\beta)}^{\mathrm{dy}} for a braid \beta of crossing number c(\beta). Birthday refines crossing number: b(\mathrm{surr}(\beta, t)) \leq c(\beta), with equality for reduced braids. The Hoefsmit factorisation equals the Conway construction: the closed formula for \rho_\lambda(\sigma_i) as a 2 \times 2 matrix in YJM coordinates is exactly the recursive surreal recipe x = \{x^- \mid x^+\}, with the eigenvalue ratio q : -q^{-1} determining the position of x. The Jones polynomial J_K(q) can be re-expressed as a weighted sum over surreal sign sequences (Jones polynomial birthday refinement). Finally, knot complexity acquires an honest ordinal-valued refinement: knots of unbounded crossing number live at birthdays approaching \omega.

The Hoefsmit seminormal form is already the algebraic-combinatorial backbone of the paper. This same backbone is shown to be a literal instance of Conway's surreal-number construction. The surreal lift of QOU is not a new structure; it is a different language for what Hoefsmit already provides.
prf:hoefsmit-is-surreal-construction:
Proof Proof of hoefsmit is surreal construction. Sketch.

The Hoefsmit seminormal basis is built by inductively decomposing V^{\otimes n} via the chain H_1(q) \subset H_2(q) \subset \cdots \subset H_n(q). At each step k, every existing eigenvector v_t for H_k(q) splits under \sigma_k into:

  • a^+_t \cdot v_{t \cup \square_{k+1}^{\to}} (extend tableau rightward; q-eigenvalue);
  • a^-_t \cdot v_{t \cup \square_{k+1}^{\downarrow}} (extend tableau downward; -q^{-1}-eigenvalue).

Conway's surreal construction at stage k takes each existing surreal x with sign-sequence s and produces exactly two new surreals: x^+ (insert + at position k+1) and x^- (insert - at position k+1). The embedding \Phi matches each tableau splitting with the corresponding sign extension step-by-step. The tableau side, however, produces the antisymmetric child only when the two-row shape constraint permits it (a box can be added to the second row of \lambda = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2) only if \lambda_2 < \lambda_1), while Conway's construction always splits both ways — which is exactly why \Phi is injective but not surjective: the unmatched sign sequences are the non-tableau dyadic rationals identified in the statement.

Compatibility with sums is forced by the eigenvalue convention: \sigma_i's q-eigenspace + -q^{-1}-eigenspace decomposition matches Conway's \{L \mid R\} pairing L < x < R.

For tableaux of shape \lambda with \ell(\lambda) \leq 2, the restriction to "first or second row" is exactly the \mathrm{SU}(2) constraint that limits Young diagrams to two-rowed shapes — giving the binary (rather than r-ary) split needed for the sign-sequence interpretation.

A full proof requires:

  • making the YJM-tableau tree structure precise (Young tableaux together with a successor relation);
  • a precise treatment of Gonshor's sign-sequence-to-surreal map;
  • checking the eigenvalue conventions (Hoefsmit uses q and -q^{-1}; Conway's construction uses left/right of midpoint).

The embedding (sign sequence functor) is therefore taken as a hypothesis pending these prerequisites.
sec:standard-part-classical-limits-intro: The standard-part map projects surreal-valued observables to their real shadows, recovering classical limits.
rem:valuation-ring-finite-surreals:
Remark Standard-part as valuation-ring projection \mathcal{O} \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m} \cong \mathbb{R}. The standard-part map \mathrm{st} : \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} \to \mathbb{R}, which sends each finite surreal x (one with |x| \leq n for some n \in \mathbb{N}) to the unique real r \in \mathbb{R} with x - r infinitesimal (|x - r| < 1/n for every n \in \mathbb{N}), admits a clean ring-theoretic reading: it is the quotient map of a valuation ring.

The finite surreals form a convex subring of \mathbf{No}:

  \mathcal{O} = \{ x \in \mathbf{No} : \exists n \in \mathbb{N},\, -n < x < n \} = \{ x \in \mathbf{No} : \mathrm{IsFinite}(x) \}.

The infinitesimals form its unique maximal ideal:

  \mathfrak{m} = \{ x \in \mathcal{O} : \mathrm{IsInfinitesimal}(x) \}.

The quotient \mathcal{O} / \mathfrak{m} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathbb{R} is canonically isomorphic to the real numbers, and the projection \mathcal{O} \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m} is exactly \mathrm{st}.

The appendix's functorial constructions (point-evaluation of schemes, categorical enrichments, surreal-coefficient sheaves) all need a set-sized coefficient ring to avoid proper-class pathologies. The valuation ring \mathcal{O} is set-sized; the ambient \mathbf{No} is a proper class. Restricting to \mathcal{O} before point-evaluation stays inside standard set-theoretic foundations.

The infinite surreals \mathbf{No} \setminus \mathcal{O} are not in the domain of \mathrm{st}. Any arithmetic involving \omega, \omega^2, \omega^\omega must be restricted to \mathcal{O} before projecting. This matches the archimedean-observability boundary already implicit in the main paper's treatment of physical observables.

The main paper develops the points-and-topology framework for QOU in its categorical-foundations chapters. In that framework, points of a categorical structure live in an R-algebra for some coefficient ring R. For the surreal setting, the natural choice is R = \mathcal{O} (finite surreals), with the archimedean quotient recovering R = \mathbb{R}. No new framework is introduced here; the Robinson standard-part construction fits the existing categorical framework.
conj:classical-limit-stpart:
Conjecture Classical-limit functor as standard-part of evaluation at q = 1 + \varepsilon. Two blocks address the q \to 1 classical limit:

Block Scope Status
classical limit functor Topological definition \mathcal{L} : \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_1 Definition (with obstruction)
This result Single-functor surreal replacement: \mathcal{L} \cong \mathrm{St} \circ \mathrm{ev}_{1+\varepsilon} Conjecture (open)

The classical limit functor \mathrm{cl} : \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_{q=1} takes the q \to 1 limit of categorical structures parametrised by the aether parameter q. Classically, this requires a topological notion of limit on the parameter space or a careful Hochschild-cohomology construction (classical limit obstruction). This conjecture proposes a clean replacement: the classical-limit functor is the standard-part of evaluation at q = 1 + \varepsilon.

Let \mathbf{C}_q be a K-linear monoidal category whose structure constants are rational functions of q \in K, and let \mathrm{cl}_{\mathrm{top}} : \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_{q=1} be the topological classical-limit functor (defined when it exists). Set K = \mathbf{No}, fix an infinitesimal \varepsilon \in \mathbf{No}, and let \mathrm{ev}_{1 + \varepsilon} : \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{No}} be evaluation at q = 1 + \varepsilon. There is a natural isomorphism of functors

  \mathrm{cl}_{\mathrm{top}} \cong \mathrm{St} \circ \mathrm{ev}_{1 + \varepsilon},

whenever the left-hand side is defined. The right-hand side is defined more generally—wherever the structure constants make sense as rational expressions in \varepsilon.

The right-hand side always exists as long as the structure constants are rational in \varepsilon, even when the left-hand side has obstructions. The classical-limit obstruction \mathrm{HH}^2(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad}) becomes a non-zero finite surreal in \mathbf{No}_{\mathrm{fin}} whose standard-part vanishes only when the obstruction itself vanishes. The obstruction is always detected in the surreal lift (as a non-trivial first-order \varepsilon-term), but it is "felt by the classical observer" only when the standard-part is non-zero.

The conjecture is open. It is partly motivated by Berarducci--Mantova's derivation construction (2018), which extends d/dx on \mathbb{R}. Promoting this from a single function to a functor on \mathbf{C}_q requires functoriality of the standard-part. A first step would be to prove the conjecture for \mathbf{C}_q = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)).

The paper treats the q \to 1 classical limit archimedean-topologically. Under the surreal lift, the limit becomes a literal evaluation at a specific surreal—no topology required. Whether the two formulations give the same answer is the conjecture above. If true, the entire classical-limit discussion could be re-stated as standard-part identities, eliminating one source of analytic machinery.

The proof strategy splits into a single-morphism case and a naturality case. For the single-morphism case, specialise to \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{Q}(q)} and a morphism given by a single rational function f_q(x). Show that \lim_{q \to 1} f_q equals \mathrm{st}(f_{1+\varepsilon}). This requires standard-part commuting with rational arithmetic on finite surreals. For naturality, generalise to a functor \mathrm{cl}_{\mathrm{top}} : \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_{q=1}. This requires functoriality of \mathrm{St} on the K-linear category \mathbf{C}_K. Falsification requires a discontinuous-but-classically-limit-existing function, which is impossible for rational structure constants.
conj:archimedean-stpart:
Conjecture Archimedean QOU is the standard-part of surreal QOU. An archimedean QOU (\mathbf{C}, \varTheta, G, \mathcal{S}) (quantum observable universe) uses K = \mathbb{R}, a real Lie group G, and a real vector bundle \mathcal{S}. A surreal QOU uses K = \mathbf{No} with all axioms relaxed to hold up to an infinitesimal \varepsilon:

Axiom Archimedean Surreal
Frobenius pairing \int_A \circ \mu = \mathrm{id} = \mathrm{id} + O(\varepsilon)
Observability \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0 \leq \varepsilon
Volume g_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id} = (1 + \varepsilon) \mathrm{id}
Vacuum \mathrm{Geom}(\bigcirc) = 0 = \varepsilon

The standard-part map \mathrm{St} sends every surreal QOU to an archimedean QOU.

More precisely, there is a functor \mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{QOU}} : \mathbf{QOU}_{\mathbf{No}}^{\varepsilon} \longrightarrow \mathbf{QOU}_{\mathbb{R}} defined by applying \mathrm{St} to all hom-spaces. The functor is essentially surjective, and the composition \mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{QOU}} \circ \iota is the identity.

If the conjecture holds, the surreal lift carries strictly more information than the archimedean theory. Each archimedean QOU has a fibre of surreal QOUs above it. The additional information is infinitesimal physics: first-order quantum corrections to the Frobenius pairing, observability cohomology, volume normalisation, and vacuum. Whether such corrections are physical or only mathematical is open.

This conjecture is the categorical counterpart of classical limit as standard-part. The two conjectures are likely equivalent modulo functoriality.

If true, the \varepsilon-relaxation is a strict generalisation of the main paper. The main paper's QOU axioms are recovered via \mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{QOU}}. Every theorem in the main paper has a surreal counterpart, potentially with non-trivial first-order corrections that vanish under \mathrm{St}.

The proof reduces to classical-limit-stpart. First, show \mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{QOU}} = (\mathrm{St}, \mathrm{St}, \mathrm{St}, \mathrm{St}). Second, reduce each component: \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}_{\mathbf{No}}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)) recovers \mathrm{Rep}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), \varTheta acts entry-wise, G is the standard-part of an algebraic group object, and \mathcal{S} is the standard-part of the fibre. Third, verify each \varepsilon-relaxed axiom becomes strict under \mathrm{St}. Finally, essential surjectivity is automatic by setting \varepsilon = 0. Falsification requires an \varepsilon-relaxed surreal QOU whose standard-part violates a strict QOU axiom.
rem:archimedean-stpart-strategy:
Remark Proof strategy for archimedean = \mathrm{St} of surreal QOU. Proof strategy for archimedean QOU is the standard-part of surreal QOU. The conjecture is the category-level counterpart of classical-limit-stpart. Reduce to that conjecture via:

  1. Functorial reduction. Show \mathrm{St}_{\mathrm{QOU}} = (\mathrm{St}, \mathrm{St}, \mathrm{St}, \mathrm{St}).
  2. Reduce each component:
    • \mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}_{\mathbf{No}}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)) at q = 1 + \varepsilon: \mathrm{St} recovers \mathrm{Rep}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) by classical-limit-stpart.
    • \varTheta : \mathbf{1} \to A: \mathrm{St} acts entry-wise.
    • G = \mathrm{Aut}(A): standard-part of an algebraic group object. This is the categorical counterpart of the archimedean realization \tau of fibre functor rigidity.
    • \mathcal{S}: standard-part of fibre.
  3. Verify axioms. Each \varepsilon-relaxed axiom becomes the strict axiom under \mathrm{St}.
  4. Essential surjectivity. Every archimedean QOU lifts (set \varepsilon = 0).

Falsification requires an \varepsilon-relaxed surreal QOU whose standard-part image violates a strict QOU axiom. This would require an infinitesimal that becomes non-infinitesimal under standard-part, which is impossible by the definition of \mathrm{st}.
thm:hyperreal-limit-transfer:
Theorem Limit transfer at \mathbb{R}^*: \mathrm{st} computes limits, and the surreal carrier is not needed.

Limit transfer, at the hyperreals, without the surreal apparatus

The appendix carries a conjecture class packaging "limits become surreal equalities": an \omega-evaluation sending each real sequence to a surreal number, compatible with the algebra and the order, and computing limits through the standard part. It is stated over the appendix's axiomatic surreal field and is not established: no model of it is exhibited.

The content needs none of that structure.

Let a_n \to L in the \varepsilon–N sense. Then, in the hyperreals \mathbb{R}^*,

  \mathrm{st}\bigl(\,{}^{*}\!a\,\bigr) \;=\; L ,

where {}^{*}\!a is the germ of the sequence at the hyperfilter. Eventual domination transfers to the hyperreal order, and the limit-comparison inequality follows from monotonicity of the standard part.

The bridge is a definitional unfolding

The corpus's notion of two surreals being infinitesimally close, applied to a hyperreal and an embedded real, unfolds to

  \forall \varepsilon > 0,\quad \lvert x - r\rvert < \varepsilon ,

which is literally the defining condition for r to be the standard part of x. The two agree by definition. So the conjecture's analytic content is the standard part of the hyperreals, and the surreal carrier plays no role in it.

⚠ What this does not do

Hyperfilter convergence is strictly weaker than convergence along \mathrm{atTop} (ordinary convergence as n \to \infty). The arrow

  a_n \to L \ \text{along } \mathrm{atTop}
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \mathrm{IsSt}({}^{*}\!a, L)

is available; the converse is false. Everything here therefore pushes real limits into \mathbb{R}^*. Nothing here proves a statement of the form \text{Tendsto} \dots \text{atTop} by a standard-part computation, because \mathrm{IsSt}({}^{*}\!a, r) says a(\omega) \approx r for one specific \omega, not for every infinite hypernatural — which is what a genuine nonstandard limit argument requires.

So surreal and standard-part machinery does not replace this corpus's \varepsilon–\delta arguments. That was the hoped-for payoff.

A defect in the surrounding axioms

Attempting to instantiate the class exposed something about the surreal-field axioms themselves. The two-valued function

  \mathrm{birthday}(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} 0 & x = 0\\ 1 & x \neq 0\end{cases}

satisfies all six birthday axioms. So those axioms do not characterise Conway's birthday; they admit a model in which every nonzero element is born on day one. In particular no lower bound on birthday is derivable from them — any statement \mathrm{birthday}(x) \ge f(x) with f unbounded is refuted by that model. Upper bounds are unaffected, which is why the bounds actually proved in the appendix survive: they are all upper bounds, and correspondingly weak.
thm:birthday-axioms-do-not-pin-the-birth:
Theorem The six birthday axioms admit a two-valued model, so they bound birthday only from above.

The six birthday axioms constrain only from above

The appendix's surreal carrier axiomatises a birthday function by six conditions. Attempting to realise them on the hyperreals exposed what they do and do not say.

The two-valued function

  \mathrm{birthday}_{\flat}(x) \;=\; \begin{cases} 0 & x = 0 \\ 1 & x \neq 0 \end{cases}

satisfies all six. So the axioms admit a model in which every nonzero element is born on day one, and the immediate consequence is a general one:

No lower bound on birthday is derivable from these axioms. Any statement \mathrm{birthday}(x) \ge f(x) with f unbounded is refuted by the flat model.

Upper bounds are untouched, which is exactly why the bounds actually proved in the appendix survive — they are all upper bounds, and correspondingly weak.

The gap in one pair of statements

For the naturals the asymmetry becomes concrete. One half is already a theorem from the existing axioms, by induction on the unit and the additivity bound:

  \mathrm{birthday}\bigl((n : \mathbb{N})\bigr) \;\le\; n .

Nothing supplies the matching \ge, and by the flat model nothing can. So the missing content is not a missing proof but a missing axiom, and it is a single equation:

  \mathrm{birthday}\bigl((n : \mathbb{N})\bigr) \;=\; n .

Why this is a mixin and not a repair of the axioms

Strengthening the carrier itself would touch every user of it, most of which never mention birthdays at all. Adding the equation as an opt-in mixin instead makes the dependency visible in the hypotheses of anything that needs genuine birthday content, and leaves the birthday-free theory — the standard-part and limit-transfer results in particular — exactly where it was. The appendix already uses this pattern elsewhere for the blow-up structure.

Combined with the inequality above, the mixin pins \mathrm{birthday}(n) exactly. It supplies only the missing half.

The independence is a theorem

The flat model fails the mixin at n = 2: two is nonzero, so \mathrm{birthday}_{\flat}(2) = 1 \neq 2. Since the flat model does satisfy all six original axioms, this is a proof that

the mixin is not derivable from them — the six axioms are satisfiable together with the negation of the added equation.

An earlier form of this claim asserted that adding the matching \ge "would kill the flat model outright". That assertion is now checked rather than asserted.

⚠ What is not claimed

That the mixin is sufficient to characterise Conway's birthday. It rules out the flat model; it does not rule out every degenerate model, and whether the strengthened axiom set is categorical is open and untouched here.

Nor does any of this bear on the appendix's standard-part theory, which never mentions birthdays — a point worth keeping separate, because the limit-transfer results are sometimes read as needing the surreal carrier when they need only its birthday-free part.

rem:conway-normal-form:
Remark Conway normal form unifies Big-O / little-o / \Theta / \sim. Every surreal x \in \mathbf{No} admits a unique Conway normal form:

  x = \sum_{i < \lambda} \omega^{y_i} \, r_i

where y_0 > y_1 > \cdots is a strictly decreasing sequence of surreals, r_i \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}, and \omega is the first infinite surreal. The sum has well-ordered support. This embeds \mathbf{No} into the Hahn field \mathbb{R}((\omega^{\mathbf{No}})).

For x \neq 0, define the leading exponent and leading coefficient:

  \ordw(x) := y_0, \qquad \mathrm{lc}(x) := r_0.

The map \ordw is a group homomorphism (\mathbf{No}^\times, \cdot) \to (\mathbf{No}, +):

  \ordw(x \cdot y) = \ordw(x) + \ordw(y).

It is the non-archimedean valuation associated to the valuation ring \mathcal{O} of finite surreals (valuation ring):

Regime Condition on \ordw(x) Meaning
x infinitesimal \ordw(x) < 0 x \in \mathfrak{m}
x finite non-inf. \ordw(x) = 0 \mathrm{st}(x) \neq 0
x infinite \ordw(x) > 0 x \notin \mathcal{O}

Classical asymptotic notation is a leading-exponent statement in disguise. For f, g evaluated at q = 1 + \varepsilon (equivalently, for f, g in the Hahn field):

Classical Surreal Proposed notation
f = O(g) \ordw(f) \leq \ordw(g) f \preceq g
f = o(g) \ordw(f) < \ordw(g) f \prec g
f = \Theta(g) \ordw(f) = \ordw(g) f \asymp g
f \sim g \ordw(f) = \ordw(g) and \mathrm{lc}(f) = \mathrm{lc}(g) f \simeq g
f = g + O(h) \ordw(f - g) \leq \ordw(h) f \equiv g \pmod{\preceq h}

Classical Big-O has three pathologies:

  1. f = O(g) is an abuse of equality; O(g) is a set.
  2. O(f) + O(g) = O(f+g) is asymmetric and not an algebraic identity.
  3. It cannot distinguish sub-polynomial behaviours: e^{-1/\varepsilon} and \varepsilon^\omega are both o(\varepsilon^n) for all n \in \mathbb{N}.

The surreal valuation replaces these with:

  1. A strict inequality \ordw(f) \leq \ordw(g) in the ordered group (\mathbf{No}, +).
  2. Algebraic laws: \ordw(f \cdot g) = \ordw(f) + \ordw(g) and \ordw(f + g) \leq \max(\ordw(f), \ordw(g)).
  3. Strict refinement by birthday. When leading exponents match, the birthday of the exponent gives an ordinal-valued depth gauge. \ordw(e^{-1/\varepsilon}) and \ordw(\varepsilon^\omega) are both negative infinite, but at different birthdays.

Example translations:

Classical Surreal
f(x) = x^2 + 5x + O(1) as x \to \infty f(x) = x^2 + 5x + r where r \prec 1
f(q) = g(q) + O((q-1)^2) as q \to 1 f \equiv g \pmod{\prec \varepsilon^2}
\int_0^1 e^{-x/\varepsilon} dx \sim \varepsilon as \varepsilon \to 0^+ \int_0^1 e^{-x/\varepsilon} dx \simeq \varepsilon

The surreal valuation serves three specific purposes in QOU:

  1. Experimental fits: Writing predictions as \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{H}} = \hat{\mathfrak{m}}_{\mathfrak{H}} + r with r \prec 1 makes the order of the residual an explicit surreal exponent rather than a hidden Big-O.
  2. Spectral gaps and singularity formation: The leading exponent determines whether a q-deformed spectral gap closes algebraically or transcendentally as q \to 1.
  3. Renormalisation counterterms: Each counterterm in the blow-up calculus has a specific leading exponent. Matching counterterms to divergences means matching leading exponents.

The appendix uses \preceq, \prec, \asymp, \simeq uniformly.

rem:surreal-blowup-examples:

In the unnormalised convention \mathrm{tr}_M(1) = 1, normalisation factors become 1/0. The named-surreal calculus makes these distinctions explicit.

The blow-up calculus respects the birthday grading. The counterterm C(\omega) has the same birthday as X(\omega). Their difference lives at a strictly lower birthday. The standard part collapses it to \mathbb{R}. This provides a birthday-graded refinement of BPHZ subtraction, where each subtraction reduces the birthday by a controlled ordinal amount.

rem:mobius-surreal-renormalization:
Remark Möbius energy as a difference of infinite surreals. The Möbius energy is a renormalized quadratic interaction: \iint |\varrho(s)-\varrho(t)|^{-2} and \iint D(s,t)^{-2} each diverge on the diagonal, and the divergences cancel. Under the surreal lift, this renormalization becomes a difference of two infinite surreals.

Excise a diagonal band of width \varepsilon = 1/\omega and set

  I_1 = \iint_{|s-t|>1/\omega}\!\frac{|\varrho'(s)|\,|\varrho'(t)|}{|\varrho(s)-\varrho(t)|^2}, \qquad I_2 = \iint_{|s-t|>1/\omega}\!\frac{|\varrho'(s)|\,|\varrho'(t)|}{D(s,t)^2}.

Both are infinite surreals of \mathrm{ord}_\omega = +1; each diverges like c\,\omega. Because |\varrho(s)-\varrho(t)| = D(s,t) + O(|s-t|^3) near the diagonal, I_1 and I_2 share the same leading coefficient c. The \omega^{+1} parts cancel, I_1 - I_2 is finite, and

  E(\varrho) = \mathrm{std}\!\bigl(I_1 - I_2\bigr).

The analytic Hadamard finite part becomes the standard part of a difference of two infinite surreals of equal leading \omega-order. The finiteness bound reduces to an algebraic leading-coefficient match [\omega^{+1}]I_1 = [\omega^{+1}]I_2.

This applies generally. For the Frostman/Riesz s-energy I_s = \iint |x-y|^{-s}, the Hausdorff dimension is the \mathrm{ord}_\omega boundary at which I_s flips from infinite to finite.

This provides surreal language for a classical renormalization. It adds no archimedean obligation: E(\varrho) is the same real number. However, while \mathbf{No} carries no Lebesgue measure, Hausdorff dimension (an exponent) and renormalized energies (a difference of infinite surreals) are surreal-native.

The aether parameter is not a global constant q \in \mathbb{R} but a section of the structure sheaf valued in \mathcal{O}:

  \varepsilon \;\in\; \Gamma(X, \mathfrak{m}_X),

where \mathfrak{m}_X \subset \mathcal{O}_X is the sheaf of infinitesimals on X(\mathcal{O}). Writing \varepsilon(x) for the stalk at a point x \in X:

  2. Standard-part global constant: \mathrm{st}(\varepsilon(x)) = 0 for all x, so the classical aether is q_{\mathrm{classical}} = 1 everywhere — matching the archimedean limit to a trivial constant.

  3. Birthday-uniform at archimedean scale: the leading surreal coefficient of \varepsilon(x) (i.e., the coefficient of \omega^{-1} in the Conway normal form) is globally constant, and equals the paper's archimedean aether deviation q_0 - 1 \approx 0.11.

  1. Halo structure: every classical real point of X is surrounded by a halo (monad) of infinitesimally-fluctuated surreal points. Under the functor X(\mathrm{st}) all halo points collapse to the classical point — but within the halo, distinct surreal fluctuations are resolved.

  3. Singularity detection: a "singularity" of this paper's QOU is a point x_0 where some quantity diverges. In the surreal lift, the divergence has a specific normal-form order \ordw(\cdot) — which, by locality, can vary in a neighbourhood of x_0.

This conjecture refines Hahn-series aether: instead of q being a single Hahn series, it is a sheaf of Hahn series. The base \mathbb{R}- shadow agrees with the paper in both cases.

It also specialises archimedean-stpart to the sheaf-theoretic setting: the archimedean QOU is the standard-part sheaf-morphism of the surreal QOU, not a single-point morphism.

conj:spectral-normal-form:
Conjecture Spectral gap closure and singularity formation as q \to 1 read from normal-form exponents. Under the surreal lift q = 1 + \varepsilon (Hahn aether), every spectral operator O_q of this paper (Hecke generators, transfer matrices, q- Hamiltonians, Feynman integrals, vortex operators) has eigenvalues \lambda_i(q) that are rational in \varepsilon, hence elements of the valuation ring \mathcal{O}.

This conjecture asserts that spectral gaps and singularities as q \to 1 are read directly off the leading exponent \ordw(\cdot) of the eigenvalues, without analytic limits.

Conjecture

Let O_q : V \to V be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional \mathbf{No}-vector space, whose matrix entries are rational functions of q. At q = 1 + \varepsilon, let

  \lambda_1(\varepsilon) \leq \lambda_2(\varepsilon) \leq \cdots
   \leq \lambda_N(\varepsilon)

be the eigenvalues ordered by \mathbf{No}-magnitude. Define the spectral gap \Delta := \lambda_2(\varepsilon) - \lambda_1(\varepsilon).

  1. Algebraic closure at q = 1: the gap \Delta closes in the classical limit iff \ordw(\Delta) < 0 (i.e., \Delta is infinitesimal).

  2. Closure rate from leading exponent: the rate of closure is \ordw(\Delta) \in \mathbf{No}. Specifically:

    • \ordw(\Delta) = 0: gap stays open in the classical limit (no closure).
    • \ordw(\Delta) = -1: gap closes linearly, \Delta \sim c\,\varepsilon — generic first-order closure.
    • \ordw(\Delta) = -n for n \in \mathbb{N}: gap closes polynomially of order n.
    • \ordw(\Delta) \in (-\omega\cdot 2,\, -\omega): gap closes faster than any polynomial but slower than any exponential — signals transcendental quantum-dilogarithm behaviour.

  3. Singularity formation: a divergence (eigenvalue blowing up) has \ordw(\lambda_i) > 0 in the surreal lift. The exponent \ordw(\lambda_i) classifies the divergence type:

    • \ordw(\lambda_i) = 1: simple pole, \lambda_i \sim C/\varepsilon = C\omega.
    • \ordw(\lambda_i) = n: n-th order pole, \lambda_i \sim C\omega^n.
    • \ordw(\lambda_i) \in (1, 2): fractional-order divergence, signalling root-of-unity or Weierstrass behaviour.

  4. Algebraic vs transcendental singularities: if \ordw(\lambda_i) is a rational surreal (in the Hahn-series rationals \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbf{No}), the singularity is algebraic. If \ordw(\lambda_i) is transfinite (involves \omega or logarithms), the singularity is transcendental.

Application to QOU

Specialise to two main-paper operators:

Categorical transfer matrix T(c, d) (braiding eigenvalues):

  • Eigenvalues are q and -q^{-1} at every Hecke-level step.
  • At q = 1 + \varepsilon: leading terms 1 + \varepsilon and -(1 - \varepsilon + \varepsilon^2 - \cdots) = -1 + \varepsilon - \varepsilon^2 + \cdots.
  • Gap \Delta = q - (-q^{-1}) = q + q^{-1}, which equals 2 + O(\varepsilon^2) at q = 1 + \varepsilon. \ordw(\Delta - 2) = -2, so no closure; the classical limit preserves the binary splitting.

q-Hamiltonian \hat{H}_q (from this paper):

  • At q = 1 + \varepsilon, each eigenvalue is rational in \varepsilon.
  • Classical-limit q \to 1 eigenvalues are the standard-parts.
  • Quantum corrections are the subleading coefficients — accessible by inverting the \ordw filtration.

Möbius energy E_q:

  • E_q = \frac{1}{4} E_{\mathrm{classical}} + \mathrm{const} at q \to 1.
  • Surreal-lifted: \ordw(E_q - \frac{1}{4}E_{\mathrm{classical}}) \geq 0, with the leading surreal constant fixed.

Contrast with classical spectral theory

Classical spectral analysis of q-deformed operators requires:

  • \varepsilon--\delta bounds on eigenvalues as q \to 1;
  • careful treatment of multiplicity crossings;
  • perturbation theory with analytic convergence radii.

Under the surreal lift, all of this is replaced by:

  • algebraic evaluation of eigenvalues at q = 1 + \varepsilon (a rational arithmetic in \varepsilon);
  • ordinal-valued leading exponents of spectral differences classifying gap closure;
  • no convergence requirement — everything is formal power series with infinite-birthday exponents.

This is a substantive conceptual simplification; whether it corresponds to a practical proof technique (replacing current spectral-gap proofs in the paper with surreal evaluations) depends on computability of the normal forms.

Proof strategy

Algebraic case (provable now, modulo conjecture Hahn-aether):

  1. Assume O_q has matrix entries in \mathbb{Q}(q) or, more generally, in the Hahn-series aether.

  2. Eigenvalues are rational functions of q by standard linear algebra; hence rational in \varepsilon at q = 1 + \varepsilon.

  3. Compute \ordw(\Delta) directly from the rational-function expression.

  4. Verify against this paper's spectral-gap statements (e.g., for the Hecke generators where the gap is known classically).

Transcendental case (speculative):

  1. For operators whose entries involve the quantum dilogarithm or other transcendentals, appeal to Berarducci–Mantova exponential/log on \mathbf{No} [berarducci-mantova2018].

  2. Compute the normal-form expansion of each eigenvalue, reading off the leading transfinite exponent.

  3. Match against known asymptotic-volume formulas (Kashaev, etc.).

Required infrastructure:

  • Rational-function arithmetic at q = 1 + \varepsilon (partial; via specialising polynomials over R_q at surreal values).
  • Hahn-series aether (pending).
  • Normal-form computation for eigenvalues (pending).

Falsification path: find an operator O_q with classically well-defined spectral gap closure not matching the leading exponent \ordw(\Delta). Such a mismatch would refute the surreal-normal-form interpretation, likely indicating a subtle multi-scale behaviour that the surreal lift does not capture.

Provability assessment: algebraic case mostly tractable with current surreal infrastructure. Transcendental case requires Berarducci–Mantova. The overall conjecture is a dictionary, more testable than deep-research-open.

Open problem

The conjecture is open. Its importance depends on whether the QOU paper's spectral-gap and singularity-formation claims can be rewritten as leading-exponent computations. If so, the classical-limit discussions simplify substantially; if not, the surreal lift is a curiosity.
conj:kashaev-surreal:
Conjecture Kashaev–Murakami–Murakami volume conjecture as a surreal standard-part identity. The Kashaev–Murakami–Murakami volume conjecture [kashaev1997] (open in full generality; provenance is recorded in that block) states:

  \mathrm{Vol}(S^3 \setminus K)
   \;=\; 2 \pi \cdot \lim_{n \to \infty}
    \frac{\log |J_K(\zeta_n, n)|}{n},

where J_K(q, n) is the n-th coloured Jones polynomial, \zeta_n = e^{2 \pi i / n}, and \mathrm{Vol} is the hyperbolic volume.

The conjecture has two awkward features when viewed through QOU:

  1. The left-hand side is hyperbolic volume — pure analytic geometry, broken under surreal replacement.
  2. The right-hand side uses an asymptotic-n limit at a root of unity — a singular limit in \mathbb{C}.

Under the surreal lift, both sides admit cleaner reformulations, and the gap between them sharpens.

Reformulation

Set n = \omega \in \mathbf{No} (the first infinite ordinal as a surreal). Then \zeta_\omega = e^{2 \pi i / \omega} is a specific element of \mathbf{No}[i] (interpreting the exponential via Berarducci--Mantova's transseries [berarducci-mantova2018]). The coloured Jones polynomial J_K(q, n) is rational in q and polynomial in n for fixed K, so J_K(\zeta_\omega, \omega) is well-defined as an element of \mathbf{No}[i].

The surreal Kashaev statement is:

  \mathrm{Vol}(S^3 \setminus K)
   \;\stackrel{?}{=}\;
   \mathrm{st}\!\left(
     2 \pi \cdot \frac{\log |J_K(\zeta_\omega, \omega)|}{\omega}
   \right),

where \mathrm{st} is the standard-part map applied to a finite surreal.

The trade-off

The reformulation does not solve the volume conjecture. It trades:

  • (classical) an analytic limit \lim_{n \to \infty} of complex numbers, plus a hyperbolic-volume identity in \mathbb{R};

for:

  • (surreal) an evaluation of a polynomial-in-n at n = \omega, plus the standard-part identity that the result agrees with hyperbolic volume.

The right-hand side of the surreal version is manifestly well-defined (rational arithmetic in \mathbf{No}), so the question reduces to whether the standard-part matches. The asymptotic-limit content of Kashaev becomes the standard-part content of the surreal version.

Location of the algebra-vs-analysis split

The reformulation makes the algebraic and analytic content of Kashaev separable:

Side Algebra-vs-analysis content
RHS, before \mathrm{st} Pure algebra: rational in \omega at root of unity
\mathrm{st} application Asymptotic transseries reduction
Identification with \mathrm{Vol} Genuine hyperbolic geometry

The first row uses no analysis. The second row uses a single transseries reduction (Berarducci--Mantova) — an instance of the \mathrm{st}/\mathrm{ord}_\omega reduction of the surreal blow-up calculus. The third row is where hyperbolic geometry enters — and it enters only on the LHS.

The second row admits a precise name from resurgence theory [ecalle1981]. The Berarducci--Mantova transseries invoked there are transseries in Écalle's sense, and the evaluation sits on a Stokes ray of the Kashaev asymptotic series, where the two lateral Borel sums of a divergent transseries disagree. The standard-part map applied to the finite surreal selects the unique real-single-valued value — which is the median resummation of Écalle's alien calculus. The unspecified "asymptotic transseries reduction" is therefore a named operation: \mathrm{st} acts as median resummation of the Kashaev transseries at the root of unity. This identifies the second row's content with a standard resurgence construction; it does not touch the third row, which remains the genuine geometric input.

The resummation step of the second row is proved for two families. For a Habiro element \Phi_K with formal series F_K(x) = \Phi_K(e^{-1/x}), the Costin--Garoufalidis conjecture asks that the Borel transform be resurgent and that the median resummation S^{\mathrm{med}}_K have radial limits recovering \Phi_K at roots of unity [crew2023, §1, Conj. 1.1]; it is proved for the torus knots T(2,2u+1) and T(3,2^k), which include the trefoil [crew2023, Cor. 1.5, via Thm. 1.4 and eq. (1.22)]. Torus knots have zero hyperbolic volume, so these cases bear on the second row only and say nothing about the \mathrm{Vol}-identity of the third row; 4_1 is outside the proved class.

Kashaev thus becomes one transseries reduction plus one \mathrm{Vol}-identity, instead of an analytic limit plus a \mathrm{Vol}-identity.

Potential utility and its limits

Might help: the algebraic side J_K(\zeta_\omega, \omega) is exactly computable for any specific knot (it is a rational function evaluated at named surreals). If a general formula exists for \mathrm{st}(\log |J_K(\zeta_\omega, \omega)|/\omega) in terms of knot data, there is a path to a proof of Kashaev.

Might not help: the standard-part identity is itself an analytic statement (it asserts an asymptotic relationship between the algebraic and the geometric). The surreal lift may just relocate the difficulty rather than dissolve it.

Discussion

Open in general; a theorem for the figure-eight knot — the conjecture is a reformulation, not a proof. Its value is in separating the algebraic content (which is computable) from the geometric content (which is the actual Kashaev). For K = 4_1 the classical limit statement is a theorem [murakami-murakami2001], so the surreal form holds with = in place of \stackrel{?}{=} for 4_1 — see the next section.

Figure-eight discharge and quantum-modularity refinement

For the figure-eight knot the two question marks collapse:

  1. Leading order (=, not \stackrel{?}{=}). The classical Kashaev limit for 4_1 is proved [murakami-murakami2001]. Combined with the formulation equivalence (proof-strategy items 1--3 below, provable by transfer), the surreal statement is a theorem for 4_1:

    2 \pi \cdot \frac{\log |J_{4_1}(\zeta_\omega, \omega)|}{\omega}
  \right)
  \;=\; \mathrm{Vol}(S^3 \setminus 4_1)

    conditional only on the transfer equivalence, not on any open conjecture.

  2. All orders (quantum modularity). Under the modular-resurgence template [fantini-rella2024] these Stokes constants are coefficients of an L-function, tying the alien calculus of the series to a quantum modular form.

The QOU relevance is concentrated at 4_1 because the muon anchor is \mathfrak{m}_\mu = \mathfrak{m}_e \cdot \mathrm{Vol}(4_1)/\hbar_q^2: the volume entering the mass formula is backed, at 4_1, by a proved equality rather than a conjectural limit.
